b7eedb20.t: So that you know who you are dealing with: I grew up on a dairy farm in the Weinviertel, thirty cows, tie stalls. My favourite cow was called Rosi, and she taught me more about feeding than my entire first semester. If the hay was no good, she simply left it – pointedly, while looking at me. I have not seen a more honest feed evaluation since.

ebe14a0a.t: My father knew this without a single lecture in farm economics. Whenever the feed merchant’s lorry pulled into the yard, he would say: ‘Here comes the man who actually gets the milk money.’ … With feed at roughly half the costs, he wasn’t far off.

79a1721d.t: After my doctorate I spent a year in Brazil on a feedlot: two thousand cattle, not a single blade of grass. Feed conversion was discussed every morning over coffee, the way we discuss the weather. Improve it by a tenth, multiply by two thousand animals and by every single day – and you are no longer talking about decimal places. You are talking about lorries.

c82bdb63.t: Quick question for the room: who is more efficient – the broiler or the dairy cow? … Most people say the chicken, and on paper they are right. But the cow mostly eats forage that we humans could not eat at all. So efficiency always depends on what you put in the denominator – do remember that, it will follow you through your entire degree.

ad9979f3.t: My grandfather used to say: ‘The dung heap is the farmer’s savings account.’ Scientifically he had a point – the nitrogen that doesn’t end up in the milk goes back to the land via slurry and manure. Unfortunately this account also pays interest into the air … in the form of ammonia.

6cc67c45.t: And what does the cow eat on all that grassland? … ‘Grass’, I hear from the back. I am afraid I must correct you on day one: grass is not a feedstuff, grass is a condition. A meadow in May and the same meadow in August are two entirely different feeds as far as the cow is concerned – you will believe me by the time we reach energy evaluation.

3f6c674f.t: Feed costs and feed conversion – that will be on the exam. Not because I am strict, but because it is the first thing you will be asked on any farm. Nobody in a farmyard will ask you about proximate analysis. They will ask: ‘And what is that going to cost me?’

3de4ed7f.t: Proximate analysis dates from the 1860s, from Weende near Göttingen. That makes it older than BOKU itself – the university was only founded in 1872. And it still works more reliably than our projector … though admittedly, that is not a high bar.

c9bcbe40.t: Crude ash is brutally honest: it contains everything that doesn’t burn – the minerals, and also whatever soil the forage wagon picked up on the way. In grass silage it should stay below about 10 percent of dry matter. When I see a good deal more than that, I ask the farmer very politely: did you mow this, or plough it?

37c1029a.t: Why 6.25, of all numbers? … Because one hundred divided by sixteen is 6.25 – protein contains on average about 16 percent nitrogen. On average, mind you: food analysts use 6.38 for milk protein and 5.7 for wheat. Feed analysis sticks with 6.25 – out of principle, out of tradition and, frankly, a little out of convenience.

8a8a1773.t: The fact that the method only counts nitrogen is not merely theoretical. In 2007, pet food turned up in North America whose protein ingredients had been spiked with melamine – and melamine is about two-thirds nitrogen. Many dogs and cats died of kidney failure. There is no punchline here, ladies and gentlemen – only the lesson that an analysis is exactly as honest as whoever supplies the feed.

2a3496af.t: Crude fibre is a bit like a badly run admissions procedure: whatever survives acid and alkali counts as fibre. But part of the lignin and the hemicellulose gets lost along the way and quietly ends up in the nitrogen-free extract. Precisely the candidates we actually wanted to meet.

71e793a9.t: NDF, ADF and ADL nest inside one another like the layers of an onion: the whole cell wall on the outside, and right at the centre only the lignin is left. That will be on the exam – as a drawing. A drawing tells me at once whether you have understood it or merely memorised it.

49d51af4.t: Wet chemistry has its hazards. As a doctoral student I once left the drying oven running over the weekend – with my lunch inside, by accident. By Monday the ham roll had reached constant weight at 103 degrees: textbook drying, analytically flawless … and utterly inedible. Which, incidentally, is precisely the difference between a feed analysis and a feed.

97b82c40.t: For us humans, incidentally, the pig is a far better role model than the cow: omnivore, simple stomach, a very similar gut. That is why it is a popular model animal in human nutrition research. So if you want to know how your own digestion works – don’t ask the cow.

979ea827.t: Pigs, by the way, are a good deal cleverer than their reputation. At the research farm we had a sow who worked out the latch on the feed dispenser in two days. It took our technician three weeks to build a new one. By the end it was not entirely clear who was experimenting on whom.

8f5c7b03.t: Amino acids released only in the large intestine are, for the pig, like a voucher that is only valid after the shop has shut. The microbes down there are delighted; the pig gets next to nothing out of it. That is exactly why we shall evaluate protein precaecally later on – up to the end of the small intestine.

7c7fe3be.t: ‘Apparent’, by the way, does not mean the pig is only pretending. The faeces also contain shed gut cells, digestive enzymes and mucus from the animal itself. So the pig pays a handling fee on every meal – and since we cannot separate it out, we charge it to the feed.

486a3d2b.t: At my grandmother’s, the hens still roamed the yard and found their own little stones. When one was slaughtered, you could tell from the gizzard where she had been: gravel from the path, a bit of brick from the barn. The gizzard is, so to speak, the chicken’s travel diary.

2aa9fa62.t: How many caeca does a chicken have? … Two. We humans have just the one, with an appendix attached that surgeons are rather keen to remove. In the caecum department, the chicken is clearly better equipped than you or I.

5d027f76.t: Three to five hours from beak to cloaca – feed passes through a broiler faster than some of us get up the hill on the 40A in the morning. … Na ja, with the 40A it is not a digestion problem. It is a timetable problem.

28bb771d.t: At the research farm we have Rudi, a steer with a rumen fistula. That is a closable port through the flank, put in by a vet under an approved protocol, and Rudi has lived with it for years, entirely unbothered. Once you have had your arm in a warm rumen up to the shoulder – about 39 degrees, very damp – you know what 160 litres means. Rudi carries on chewing throughout. He has more patience with students than I do.

1e04c5cf.t: I wrote my doctoral thesis on rumen protozoa – single-celled creatures that look under the microscope like hairy potatoes in a hurry. There are far fewer of them than bacteria, but they are so large that they still make up a considerable share of the microbial mass. I spent three years counting them. My mother never quite understood why – after all, Rosi had managed perfectly well without a doctorate.

79b0bb72.t: Which makes the cow the only enterprise on earth that turns vinegar into butter. … Yes, that is simplified, but it isn’t wrong: the udder builds a good share of the milk fatty acids from acetic acid. No chemist manages that so elegantly – and certainly not with hay and silage as raw material.

ad150e3c.t: How do you measure rumen pH in a cow who won’t tell you? … The old way was a stomach tube – but you tend to pull up saliva with it, which flatters the result. Today some cows carry a pH bolus in the reticulum that radios a reading every few minutes. The cow, in other words, is now more digital than many a lecture theatre.

9bfaea78.t: Every evening my father went back into the barn just to see whether the cows were lying down and chewing the cud. If they were, he said ‘Right then’ and went to bed. Today a sensor on a neck collar does that and sends a message to your phone. Same principle – except the farmer now sleeps worse, because the phone keeps beeping.

e7cd56a7.t: The shaker box is the only piece of lab equipment you operate with your whole body: five shakes, a quarter turn, eight times round – forty shakes in all. I have seen students come out of three samples fitter than after a semester of university sport. And the cow? She chews the cud next to you and keeps her opinions to herself.

34932ce2.t: For the bomb calorimeter the sample is dried and pressed into a small pellet. As a student I once did that sloppily – result: incomplete combustion, soot in the crucible, and a lab assistant whose expression I remember to this day. That was my first lesson in gross energy: what doesn’t burn doesn’t count.

a0e44768.t: Which has more gross energy – a kilo of butter or a kilo of hay? … The butter, almost twice as much, because fat delivers about 39 megajoules per kilo. Yet no cow would get far on butter: more than about 5 percent fat in the ration and fibre digestion in the rumen goes on strike. Energy is not what is in it – it is what arrives.

5aa9b861.t: Whenever I think of the energy cascade, I think of my Kaspressknödel – cheese dumplings – in the refectory. Gross energy: considerable. Metabolisable energy: still respectable. And how much net energy is left over for teaching at the two o’clock lecture … I shall leave that for you to judge.

67b55a6a.t: A hundred and thirty-six megajoules a day – just for scale: an adult human gets by on about 10. So the cow needs more than ten times as much, and that is net energy, after all the losses. Feeding a high-yielding cow is essentially looking after a professional athlete – one with about three hundred competition days a year.

6b64e455.t: These values – hay, grass silage, maize silage, barley – will be on the exam. Not to the decimal place, but in the right order. Anyone who writes that hay has more energy than barley won’t get the mark – but will receive a warm invitation to come and turn hay.

7c688edc.t: In poultry everything leaves through a single exit – which is handy for the analyst: one sample pot instead of two. For whoever collects the samples, let me put it diplomatically: one gets used to a great deal. Over three trials I got used to everything … except the smell.

53e62cfa.t: Rudi is perfect for demonstrating this: we hang little nylon bags of soybean meal into the rumen through the fistula and check after a few hours how much protein is left. That is the in situ method, and it is how many degradability values get into the tables. Rudi is the most patient member of staff on the entire research farm. He draws no salary – but he does get the best ration.

1cd8aaa0.t: Rumen microbes have a remarkable career: they work round the clock, train up their own successors – and when they are washed into the abomasum with the digesta, they are digested. As high-quality protein, at least. A career with a rather short retirement.

a0b106d2.t: Where does the cow get her protein, if not directly from the feed? … The protein reaching the small intestine usually comes more than half from rumen microbes. So when you drink milk, you are drinking protein that has been through bacteria. I find that wonderful – my children still find it slightly revolting. Possibly one reason neither of them went into farming.

c5f9238f.t: The cow was recycling long before it was fashionable: urea from the liver goes back to the microbes via saliva and the rumen wall, and they turn it into protein again. When protein is scarce, she can reuse a considerable share of her nitrogen this way. I once called it ‘the circular economy on four legs’ in a lecture. A week later it was on a poster in the corridor – without a citation.

1b875075.t: On the feedlot in Brazil, feed-grade urea stood in big sacks in the store – there is no cheaper nitrogen. But careful, it is all about the dose: too much at once, or without adaptation, and ammonia floods into the blood faster than the liver can cope. That is where I learned to introduce urea gradually and mix it in thoroughly. And to lock the store – not because of thieves, but because of curious cattle.

6254fb05.t: Fifteen to twenty-five milligrams per hundred millilitres – that will be on the exam. And after that it will be in the milk recording report every month for your entire career. You pass the exam once; the recording report stays with you for thirty years.

084058c9.t: Picture a building site: bricks piled up everywhere – that is the nitrogen. But the bricklayers have had no lunch – that is the missing energy. So nothing gets built, and in the end the bricks are carted away again … via the liver and the urine.

e0af7d17.t: Why is it methionine, of all things, that runs short first in poultry? … Feathers! Feathers are almost pure keratin, which is rich in sulphur amino acids, above all cystine – and the bird makes cystine from methionine. In a sense, a chicken wears its methionine requirement as a coat.

0727fb36.t: I only truly understood Liebig’s barrel when the old rain barrel at home had a cracked stave. The water stood exactly up to the crack, not an inch higher. My father said: ‘See – no use the other boards being longer.’ The man never read a line of Liebig and still gave the lecture.

0127ac91.t: Why is everything expressed relative to lysine? … Because in pigs lysine is almost always the first to run short, and because it is easy to analyse and to supplement precisely. Lysine is the reserve currency, so to speak – the other amino acids are converted into it, much as we Austrians used to convert everything into schillings. Some of us still do.

2020b7b8.t: At home we kept a few pigs for the household, and they got one single feed from piglet to slaughter. Simple, certainly – except the young ones had rather too little protein and the older ones too much. The surplus turned up again in the slurry pit. We didn’t know that at the time … we could smell it, though.

9c0eac73.t: I was going to show you a video of how lysine is made – but the projector and I are never going to be friends. So, verbally: L-lysine, threonine and tryptophan are produced by bacteria in enormous fermenters; only DL-methionine traditionally comes from chemical synthesis. So the lysine in pig feed was made by microbes too – just like in the rumen, only with stainless steel round it.

14377f33.t: Cereals contain plenty of phosphorus that the pig can barely get at – roughly two-thirds of it is bound as phytate. So the pig is sitting at a laid table with a glass cloche over the food. And phytase is the waiter who lifts the cloche.

28b35018.t: And before anyone says ‘grass’ – you know what is coming: grass is not a feedstuff, grass is a condition. Now you can see why: the feed tables list several rows for meadow growth, depending on cut and stage. The cow notices the difference at the first bite – we need a laboratory for it.

942e8c65.t: My father always said: ‘Hay doesn’t get any better for standing longer.’ And every year he left it standing anyway, until the weather played along. Scientifically he was right; in practice, the weather was right. To this day it is the most honest summary of grassland farming I know.

1aef760d.t: It happened to me as a doctoral student: on paper I allotted a trial cow sixty kilos of grass silage dry matter – I had mixed up fresh matter and dry matter. My supervisor merely asked whether we had started feeding elephants. A dairy cow realistically manages twenty to twenty-five kilos of dry matter a day. Since then I write ‘fresh’ or ‘dry’ next to every figure – even on my shopping list.

3f95d9b1.t: Young pasture has so little dry matter that a cow has to bite off well over a hundred kilos of fresh herbage to get twenty kilos of dry matter. And then people wonder why cows spend all day walking about with their heads down. That is not leisure, ladies and gentlemen – that is shift work.

f8fe8f11.t: So why not use rapeseed instead of soya everywhere? … In Austrian dairy feeding that is very much what happens, and it works splendidly. In pigs and poultry it is trickier: less lysine, more fibre, and the glucosinolates on top. Rapeseed is an excellent team player – but not a substitute for every position.

19fea6ae.t: By-products are the recycling department of feed science: bran from the mill, brewers’ grains from the brewery, beet pulp from the sugar factory. The leftover Kaspressknödel from the refectory, however, may not go into the trough – feeding catering waste to farm animals is banned in the EU. And for good reason: food scraps have spread animal diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease before.

e5ff63d5.t: Yes, I have just said ‘grass’ myself. You know what is coming: grass is not a feedstuff, grass is a condition. And conserving forage means nothing other than preserving that condition as well as possible – ideally the young one, not the overmature one.

1115a274.t: At the research farm we once measured the density in the bunker silo with core samples. The target for grass silage, depending on dry matter, is roughly 200 kilos of dry matter per cubic metre. Exactly where I, as a young assistant, had been rolling and had climbed down for a sandwich, we found a hole in the statistics – and mould the following winter. Since then I only eat once the sheet is on.

c4da8ee4.t: Clostridial spores are tough: they survive the rumen, the gut and even pasteurisation. That is why many hard-cheese dairies still insist on silage-free milk. A cheesemaker once told me: ‘You can’t taste bad silage in the milk – you see it months later in the cheese.’

82847714.t: How do you detect aerobic heating without instruments? … Put your hand into the silage face. If it is warmer in there than in your coat pocket, the yeasts have already been at work. At the research farm we once measured over thirty degrees in a silage in February – the farm cats greatly appreciated it, the cows rather less.

bd871aca.t: Bringing in the hay was a family affair at home, run by the weather forecast: if there was a cloud on the horizon, even my grandmother climbed onto the wagon. Hay stored too damp doesn’t just go mouldy – it can heat up until it catches fire by itself. We never joked about hay fires at home, and I am not going to start now.

5a70f6c8.t: Hay milk is an Austrian speciality that warms my ruminant-loving heart: no silage, plenty of forage, and since 2016 it has been protected across the EU as a traditional speciality guaranteed. The principle was really invented by cheesemakers – because of those very clostridia. Sometimes tradition is simply applied microbiology that nobody bothered to call by that name.

fe701563.t: You needn’t memorise the DLG scoring key, but you must be able to apply it. That will be on the exam – with a fermentation acid profile I have invented myself. I shall only tell you this much: the silage smells faintly of butyric acid even on paper.

93b55f8f.t: I'll note this on the board: of the nitrogen a dairy cow eats, only about a quarter turns up again in the milk. The large remainder goes into faeces and urine.

91991b21.t: For Austria this is especially important: almost half of our farmland is permanent grassland, plus the alpine pastures. Humans can practically only use that for food via the ruminant.

350f3314.t: Feed accounts for about half of the costs in dairy and usually more than half in pig fattening.

40416eeb.t: Nobody measures the nitrogen-free extract – NFE is simply what's left: DM minus ash, protein, fat and fibre. So all analytical errors end up right there.

570a5cb0.t: Exactly this weakness of crude fibre led to the Van Soest analysis. Instead of acid and alkali, it uses detergents and separates the cell wall more cleanly into its components.

7ace8715.t: Let me write up the three fractions: NDF is the entire cell wall, so hemicellulose, cellulose and lignin. ADF is cellulose plus lignin, and ADL is practically the lignin.

24cea5d1.t: NDF is the entire cell wall; ADF only contains cellulose and lignin, ADL essentially lignin.

6ab38541.t: And the speed – let me write it: in fattening pigs feed takes roughly 30 to 40 hours through the gut, in broilers only about 3 to 5 hours. So it has to be easily digestible.

e6860ba6.t: The crop stores, the proventriculus secretes acid and pepsin, the gizzard grinds.

a30efbf8.t: Rumen pH should be roughly between 6.2 and 7. If it stays below 5.8 for more than about five hours a day, we speak of subacute ruminal acidosis, SARA for short.

1fa68f78.t: The cause is almost always too much rapidly degradable starch and too little structure. The consequences: fluctuating intake, falling milk fat, loose faeces and often hoof problems later.

a030ccae.t: Let me write up the countermeasure: structure. Physically effective NDF stimulates rumination, seven to ten hours a day, and the cow produces 100 to 200 litres of saliva in the process.

1973322e.t: peNDF is the part of NDF in sufficiently long particles, checked for example with the shaker box. As a lower limit, roughly 18 percent peNDF above eight millimetres in ration DM applies.

d5aff7e8.t: One more by-product of fermentation for the board: methane. Archaea make CH4 from CO2 and hydrogen, and the cow loses about 6 to 7 percent of her gross energy that way.

1235d76d.t: Forage-rich rations mainly yield acetate; propionate is about 15–25 %, butyrate 10–15 %.

cc1d6378.t: About 6.2–7.0 is normal; SARA is present when pH falls below 5.8 for more than about 5 h/day.

6aae44b6.t: 18 kg × 18.5 MJ = 333 MJ GE; 333 MJ × 0.06 ≈ 20 MJ as methane.

c756ac36.t: Energy is the first bottleneck in almost every ration. The starting point is gross energy, which we measure in a bomb calorimeter by burning the sample completely.

9401aa2f.t: Wood, by the way, has a gross energy similar to hay – still, no cow has ever given milk from wood chips. What matters is how much is digested and metabolised.

b7039d65.t: Subtract the energy in faeces and we have digestible energy, DE. Subtract urine and – important in ruminants – methane, and we arrive at metabolisable energy, ME.

c153878f.t: Metabolism also produces heat, and what's left after that is net energy. For dairy cows that's NEL – of the ME, only about 60 percent ends up in the milk.

45cd06c7.t: Now the requirement, let me write it up: for maintenance a cow needs 0.293 MJ NEL per kilo of metabolic body weight, BW to the 0.75 – for 650 kilos almost 38 MJ.

c35d46e4.t: Let me write up the formula for milk: 1.05 plus 0.38 times fat plus 0.21 times protein. At 4.0 percent fat and 3.4 percent protein that gives 3.28 MJ NEL per kilo of milk.

bf280f6f.t: So our 650-kilo cow with 30 kilos of milk needs about 136 MJ NEL a day. The GfE recommendations of 2023 already work in ME, but in practice NEL is still standard in many places.

b49b315f.t: Let's look at typical contents: first-cut hay is at about 5.3 to 5.9 MJ NEL per kilo DM, good grass silage at around 6.3, maize silage at about 6.6 and barley at around 8.

d26272e8.t: In pigs we evaluate in metabolisable energy, ME. Barley has about 12.6 MJ ME per kilo of feed at 88 percent DM, wheat about 13.8 and grain maize just over 14.

65858b0c.t: In poultry, faeces and urine leave the cloaca together – let me write it up. So we measure metabolisable energy directly and correct it to zero nitrogen balance: AMEn.

513ed485.t: Faeces and urine are excreted together via the cloaca, so ME is determined directly, corrected for N.

1d2782a6.t: DE = GE − faeces; ME = DE − urine − methane; only NE deducts the heat losses.

9b5f43ed.t: With protein we have to bring two things together: crude protein from the Weende analysis and the microbes in the rumen. Because in the cow, what reaches the gut isn't what was in the feed.

ba631a31.t: Part of the feed protein is degraded in the rumen, that's RDP – all the way down to ammonia. The rest, UDP, passes the rumen unchanged and goes straight to the small intestine.

8e4d6b45.t: From ammonia the microbes build their own protein – provided they have enough energy. As a rule of thumb, we reckon with about 10 grams of microbial protein per MJ ME.

6e3a8f61.t: That gives us uCP, or nXP in German – let me write it up: utilisable crude protein at the duodenum, microbial protein plus UDP. A cow needs about 85 grams per kilo of milk.

a65788c7.t: Now the ruminal nitrogen balance, let me write it up: RNB equals CP minus uCP, divided by 6.25. The result is in grams of nitrogen and tells us whether the rumen microbes have enough N.

4760fbbd.t: In the table you can see: grass silage has a positive RNB, maize silage a clearly negative one of about minus 10. The two complement each other – the total ration shouldn't fall below zero.

62f773a3.t: What happens to excess ammonia? It passes through the rumen wall into the blood and the liver turns it into urea – some returns via saliva, the rest goes into urine and milk.

17e1021a.t: That's why you can even feed urea to ruminants – with her microbes, the cow turns a nitrogen fertiliser into protein. No pig could pull that off.

c2e75503.t: Since urea passes into milk, it's a good monitoring tool. Let me write it up: about 15 to 25 mg per 100 ml is optimal, above 30 suggests a protein surplus, below 15 a deficiency.

17ca65f4.t: Always assess urea together with milk protein, because that reflects energy supply. High urea with low milk protein often means: the microbes are short of energy.

8478478b.t: uCP is the sum of microbial protein and undegraded feed protein (UDP) at the duodenum.

4f73da11.t: 15–25 mg/100 ml is considered optimal; above 30 suggests a protein surplus, below 15 a deficiency.

8a8d1956.t: In the cow, the rumen microbes remodel the feed protein. Pigs and chickens don't have this buffer – for them, every single amino acid in the feed counts.

89a9cfb8.t: Essential amino acids are those the animal can't synthesise: lysine, methionine, threonine, tryptophan, valine and a few more. We evaluate them as precaecally digestible, up to the end of the small intestine.

aeed443c.t: Let me write up the principle: Liebig's law of the minimum. The scarcest amino acid limits protein deposition – in pigs on cereal-soy diets usually lysine, in poultry methionine.

b1765db1.t: On the slide you see the barrel: the water runs out over the shortest stave. Liebig formulated this for plants – the pig has never heard of him, but sticks to it anyway.

9576614b.t: From this follows ideal protein, let me write it up: lysine equals 100, the others in a fixed ratio to it – about 60 for methionine plus cystine, 65 for threonine, 18 for tryptophan.
